newsitem.title: IRAQ: UN says no more Iraqi missile parts excavated.
newsitem.headline: UN says no more Iraqi missile parts excavated.

text.p: Fresh Iraqi excavations have failed to unearth more wreckage of its banned missiles, a U.N. official said on Thursday.

"They (Iraqis) have not uncovered any more missile parts since the arrival of a new team of U.N. inspectors," Roger Knight, assistant director of Baghdad's Ongoing Monitoring and Verification (OMV) centre, told Reuters.
A small U.N. missile team arrived on Friday to supervise excavations at sites where the Iraqis say they destroyed and buried a large number of long-range missiles in 1992.
Knight said the latest excavations were at the same site where Iraq uncovered four wrecked rocket engines and other components in January under U.N. supervision.
Under the terms that ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait, Iraq must rid itself of missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).

Iraq is trying to prove all its banned missiles were destroyed. Knight said the significance of the finds would only be known after "a thorough examination" by U.N. experts of uncovered missile components.

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction suspects Baghdad still conceals a considerable number of banned missiles. Iraq has denied the accusation.

Iraq and UNSCOM are locked in a dispute over 100 missile engines dug up last year from another site. The commission wants to move the engines to the United States for analysis to prove they are not substitutes for the original Russian-made engines.

Iraq insists on having them examined either in Russia or France. Knight said the Iraqis were refusing to discuss removal of the engines until the visit by UNSCOM's chairman Rolf Ekeus to Baghdad on February 20.
The official newspaper al-Iraq on Tuesday accused Ekeus of "aggressive remarks" and attempts to raise tension with Iraq.
UNSCOM must certify that Iraqi weapons of mass destruction are gone before the United Nations will lift curbs on the sale of Iraqi oil.
Iraq is currently exporting limited amounts under an oil-for-food deal with U.N. which is exempt from the sanctions imposed on Baghdad for invading Kuwait in 1990.
